passage: I'm Keerthana, the neighbour across the landing, and I watched Anand from our open door. Anand's Amma had called out two jobs: blocks into the box, and finish the drawing before the food came. Anand laid the jobs out like two toys, chose the drawing because the crayons were already out, and coloured half a sun. Then a ball rolled past. The crayon dropped, and the blocks sat in their heap while the ball bounced. When the smell of dal reached the room, Anand stared at the half sun and started carrying blocks over, one by one.

qa.q: Which job did Anand choose to do first?
qa.a: Anand chose the drawing, because the crayons were already out.

qa.q: What might Anand have been feeling when the ball rolled past?
qa.a: Excited and pulled away: the crayon dropped at once, which suggests the ball felt far more fun than the half sun. Only Anand knows for sure.

qa.q: What small step could Anand's Amma try to help the plan hold next time?
qa.a: Let Anand point to the job that goes first, and move the ball out of sight until that job is done, so something shinier does not undo the choice.

qa.q: How does Keerthana make sense of the dropped crayon?
qa.a: Keerthana sees it as ordinary for a young child: putting jobs in order is new, and a bouncing ball easily beats a half-coloured sun.

grounding: A small child picks which job to do first by what is nearest and fun, and the order changes when a shinier thing appears.

passage:
Monday: Uma lined her tidy-up jobs along the rug, teddies first because teddies were her favourite. Halfway, the phone played a song and she ran off to dance. The teddies stayed in a heap.

Wednesday: her father Mohit asked, “What first, Uma?” She pointed at the crayons, then spotted a ladybird on the window and forgot the crayons for a long while.

Saturday: Uma put the crayon box on the table and announced, “Drawing first.” The ladybird crawled by again. “Bye-bye, later,” she whispered, and kept colouring. Mohit clapped once, very quietly, so as not to break her attention.

qa.q: What did Uma announce on Saturday?
qa.a: On Saturday Uma announced, “Drawing first.”

qa.q: Why might Uma have whispered “Bye-bye, later” to the ladybird?
qa.a: She wanted to keep looking at the ladybird but also wanted to finish her drawing, so she was saying goodbye to the shiny thing for now. She seems proud and a little tempted at once. 🙂

qa.q: What could Mohit try next to help Uma keep choosing an order?
qa.a: Keep asking “What first?” before each job and praise the choosing itself, since putting things in order is still new for Uma.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when he claps quietly on Saturday?
qa.a: Mohit is probably pleased and hopeful, and he wants Uma to keep her focus, which is why he claps softly instead of loudly.

grounding: A young child chooses what to do first by fun and drops the plan when something shinier appears, over several days.

passage: Imran dropped his school bag by the door. “Sums after,” he told Amma, and ran to the lane, where Uma was already calling for a fourth player. Cricket lasted until the sky went orange. Then tea, then a cartoon on the neighbour's set, and then the power went out with twelve maths sums still unopened. Imran solved three by torchlight, his eyes stinging, before Amma said, “Sleep. Tomorrow the master will ask.” The next morning he stood at the board with three sums done and nine blank lines, and the master kept him in at break to finish. Walking back to class, Imran thought: the long sums should come before the cricket.

qa.q: How many maths sums did Imran solve by torchlight?
qa.a: Imran solved three sums by torchlight.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he walked back to class after break?
qa.a: Regretful and a little embarrassed. He had sincerely believed there would be time, and his thought about doing the long sums before cricket shows he now sees the mistake.

qa.q: What could Imran try tomorrow so the evening goes differently?
qa.a: Do the twelve sums right after getting home, before going to the lane, then play cricket as the reward.

qa.q: How might Uma see Imran's evening if Uma heard about it?
qa.a: Uma might feel sorry for Imran, since Uma was the one calling for a fourth player, and might offer to call Imran only once the sums are done.

grounding: A schoolchild plays first, believing study can wait, and a bad evening and a next-day consequence teach that the hard task may need to come first.

passage: Nkechi and Ulla kicked a football around the park until the streetlamps came on. “Spelling later,” Nkechi said, waving the list of fifteen words in her pocket. At home there was rain on the windows and rice on the table, and by the time her plate was clean her eyes were heavy. She wrote out five words with her head on her hand and went to bed. On Friday the test came back with six words wrong, and Nkechi stared at the red marks. On Thursday of the next week she sat at the kitchen table before shoes and park, and finished the spellings first. The park felt better after that.

qa.q: How many words were on Nkechi's spelling list?
qa.a: There were fifteen words on Nkechi's spelling list.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi stare at the red marks on Friday?
qa.a: Nkechi was probably disappointed and surprised: she had been sure there would be time for spelling later, and the six wrong words showed otherwise.

qa.q: What did Nkechi change the following week, and what was the result?
qa.a: Nkechi did the spellings at the kitchen table before going out, and the park felt better afterwards because the work was already done.

qa.q: What would Ulla have seen if Nkechi had stayed at the park again?
qa.a: Ulla would probably have had someone to play football with again but Nkechi might have arrived at the next test tired and unprepared, so the same bad evening could repeat.

grounding: A schoolchild chooses play before homework and learns through a poor test result to do the dull task first.

passage: The house was full of drums that Friday, because Tanuja's cousin's wedding party had started early downstairs, but the physics exam was on Monday. Tanuja told herself she would revise as soon as things settled. First she answered forty messages in the class group. Then she replied to Sunaina about the poster colours, watered the balcony plants, folded the laundry and cleared her inbox down to zero. By nine the phone was quiet and the room felt tidy and finished. Under a pile of dupattas, the physics book was still shut. Tanuja looked at it and felt a small, heavy drop in her stomach. 😟

qa.q: What did Tanuja do before nine o'clock that evening?
qa.a: Tanuja answered forty messages in the class group, replied to Sunaina, watered the balcony plants, folded the laundry and cleared her inbox.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel when she saw the shut physics book?
qa.a: A small heavy drop of worry in her stomach: the busy evening had felt productive, but the exam task was still untouched.

qa.q: What could Tanuja do at nine o'clock to protect the exam revision?
qa.a: Turn the phone face down, open the book and do one small chapter section first, before any more messages or chores.

qa.q: How does Sunaina's message about poster colours fit into the evening?
qa.a: It was one more loud, small request that Tanuja answered quickly, and answering it felt useful even though it did not move the physics revision forward.

grounding: A teenager answers every message and does small chores while the important exam revision slides.

passage: On the study table Thomas wrote a to-do list: sort desk, reply to Joseph, iron uniform, charge earphones, chemistry ch. 6 revision. He did the first four in order, ticking each one with a flourish, and felt like a man in charge. The desk was spotless. Joseph had replied twice with jokes, and Thomas answered both. Uniform pressed, earphones full. The clock said ten past nine. Chemistry, last on the list, was tomorrow's quiz on six pages he had not read. Thomas rubbed his eyes, opened the book and took one long breath. “Should have started with you,” he muttered, reading the first line twice.

qa.q: What was the last item on Thomas's to-do list?
qa.a: The last item on Thomas's list was chemistry chapter 6 revision.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel as he ticked off the first four jobs?
qa.a: Thomas felt capable and in charge; the tidy desk and the ticks gave him a sense of progress even though the important task was untouched.

qa.q: What could Thomas change about how he writes his list tomorrow?
qa.a: Put chemistry first and give it a fixed start time, leaving the desk, the uniform and the replies for after.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the delayed replies and jokes?
qa.a: Joseph probably sees someone chatting cheerfully, and does not know the jokes are taking time from Thomas's chemistry.

grounding: A teenager does small urgent tasks first while important revision keeps waiting.

passage: Counsellor's note, 14 March. I'm Elizabeth, the faculty mentor for third-year students, and I met Farida today. Farida's list this week runs to seven items, all marked urgent: two assignments due Friday, aptitude test practice, a mock interview, a mother's call every evening, and a roommate's birthday. Farida has started every item and finished none, and handed me an assignment with half its answers blank. Her hands were shaking a little when she showed me the list. I did not add advice. I asked which two things she could finish well by Friday if the other five had to wait. She sat quietly, then circled the assignments and the call home. We agreed she would tell her roommate she can join for cake only.

qa.q: What day are the two assignments due?
qa.a: The two assignments are due on Friday.

qa.q: What might Farida have been feeling when her hands shook while showing the list?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and anxious: seven things all felt equally pressing, and she had finished none of them.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: Farida circled the assignments and the call home, which meant the aptitude practice, mock interview and most of the birthday plans would wait.

qa.q: How might Farida's roommate feel about hearing that Farida can only join for cake?
qa.a: The roommate may feel a little disappointed at first, but would probably still be glad Farida is coming to the birthday at all.

grounding: A college student treats every task as equally urgent and finishes none until ranking forces something to be left undone.

passage: Sunday, 11 pm. Tonight I wrote everything in red: the two assignments, mock interview prep, the placement form, Amma's call, Simran's farewell dinner, my own laundry. All urgent. I spent three hours hopping between them. The first assignment is half done, the second has a title, the interview prep is a folder with nothing in it. Amma's call was ten rushed minutes and Simran's dinner I skipped altogether, and I feel awful about that. Nothing got my full attention, and everything got a bit of my worry. Maybe if I decide what really matters I have to accept something goes undone. Tomorrow: the first assignment, then Amma, and I'll tell Simran sorry. — Dolma

qa.q: What did Dolma write in red on Sunday night?
qa.a: Dolma wrote the two assignments, mock interview prep, the placement form, Amma's call, Simran's farewell dinner and laundry, all in red.

qa.q: Why does Dolma feel awful at eleven at night?
qa.a: Dolma feels guilty about skipping Simran's dinner and about the rushed call, and also worried because nothing got full attention.

qa.q: What decision does Dolma make for tomorrow?
qa.a: Dolma decides to do the first assignment, then call Amma, and to apologise to Simran, accepting that other things will wait. 🙂

qa.q: How might Simran feel about Dolma missing the farewell dinner?
qa.a: Simran was probably disappointed to see an empty seat, but a clear apology would help Simran understand that Dolma was overloaded, not uncaring.

grounding: A college student marks every task urgent, does none well, and starts to see that ranking means leaving something undone.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage: Thursday. My report is due Friday noon, and today Parveen asked if I could tidy the slides for the team outing. It would take an hour, and I said, “I can't today, Friday's report has to go first. Ask me next week?” My face went warm. Parveen said “okay” in a flat voice, and my chest felt tight for a while. Then I put on headphones and worked from ten to twelve without opening chat. The results section is done, with the numbers checked. I still feel a little rude and I keep replaying the flat “okay”. But the report will not be crowded out by slides. I'll bring biscuits next week, and do the slides then. — Ira

qa.q: What hours did Ira work with headphones on?
qa.a: Ira worked from ten to twelve with headphones on and chat closed.

qa.q: Why does Ira keep replaying Parveen's flat “okay”?
qa.a: Ira feels guilty and a little rude for refusing, and worries the request has left Parveen upset.

qa.q: What did Ira gain by saying no, and what did it cost?
qa.a: The results section got finished and checked, which protects the Friday deadline; the cost was a moment of awkwardness and some guilt.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when asking for the slide help?
qa.a: Parveen probably felt hopeful that a quick favour would be granted, then a bit let down, though “next week” leaves the door open.

grounding: A young professional declines a low-value request to protect time for a deadline task and feels guilt about it.

subtype: Saying no to protect the main goal [Actor]
passage:
Tejas: hey, can you help me rename 300 old files today? shouldn't take long
Alka: I'd love to but I can't today 🙏 the client proposal goes out Thursday and I've blocked the afternoon
Tejas: it's only the archive folder
Alka: I know. sorry, hope that doesn't sound rude, I just can't split my attention
Tejas: hmm ok
Alka: I can do half an hour on Friday, after it's sent. deal?
Tejas: fine. friday 4?
Alka: friday 4. thank you for understanding 🙂
(Alka mutes chat, writes “no calls till 5” on a sticky note and finishes the pricing table by four.)

qa.q: When does Alka offer to help with the files?
qa.a: Alka offers half an hour on Friday, after the proposal is sent.

qa.q: Why does Alka add “hope that doesn't sound rude”?
qa.a: Alka feels a bit uneasy and guilty about refusing, and is worried it may sound unkind even though Alka feels the proposal must come first.

qa.q: What did Alka do after the chat to protect the afternoon?
qa.a: Alka muted chat, wrote “no calls till 5” on a sticky note and finished the pricing table by four.

qa.q: What might Tejas be feeling when writing “hmm ok”?
qa.a: Tejas is likely a little disappointed or brushed off, since the job seemed small, though Alka's Friday offer helps ease that.

grounding: A young professional refuses a low-value request, feels slightly rude, and protects time for a deadline-critical task.

passage: Monday, 8:45, in the dispatch office. Vijay stood at the whiteboard and wrote three lines: sign the courier contract, finish the training plan, clear the backlog of invoices. Neelam came over with her own list, fourteen lines long, and raised an eyebrow. “Fourteen never gets finished,” Vijay said. “Three might.” Each evening at six Vijay ticked what was done and rubbed out nothing. On Wednesday a truck broke down and ate the whole afternoon, so the invoices slipped. By Friday the contract was signed and the training plan was sent, and beside the invoices Vijay wrote “Monday, first”. Neelam copied the three-line idea onto a sticky note that evening.

qa.q: What three outcomes did Vijay write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Vijay wrote: sign the courier contract, finish the training plan, and clear the backlog of invoices.

qa.q: What does Vijay's calm explanation to Neelam show about Vijay's view of long lists?
qa.a: Vijay feels that a long list weighs people down and rarely gets finished, and prefers three lines that might really be done.

qa.q: What went wrong on Wednesday, and how did Vijay handle it?
qa.a: A truck broke down and took the afternoon, so the invoices slipped; Vijay simply moved them to “Monday, first” instead of abandoning the list.

qa.q: Why might Neelam have copied the three-line idea onto a sticky note?
qa.a: Neelam may feel weighed down by fourteen items and is impressed that Vijay's short list survived a bad day.

grounding: A wise planner picks three outcomes for the week, writes them down and checks them every evening.

passage:
Dear Ishita,

You asked how I stop the week running away from me. On Sunday evening I take a small card and write three outcomes, not tasks, that would make the week a good one: the vendor quote sent, the leave roster fixed, my mother's papers filed. Then I stick it on the monitor. Every evening I look at it for two minutes and tick what moved. Last week the quote and the roster got done; the papers did not, and I moved them to next week without a fuss. Before I used the card, I kept a list of twenty things and felt guilty by Tuesday. Try it for two weeks and write back.

Lalit

qa.q: Where does Lalit stick the card?
qa.a: Lalit sticks the card on the monitor.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the old twenty-item list?
qa.a: Lalit felt guilty by Tuesday, because twenty things could not be finished and the list only piled up blame.

qa.q: What did Lalit do when the mother's papers were not filed?
qa.a: Lalit moved the papers to next week without fuss and kept the card going.

qa.q: Why might Ishita have asked Lalit about running away weeks?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels swamped by too many tasks and hopes for a simple method, so a small card may feel doable. 🙂

grounding: A wise planner chooses three weekly outcomes, writes them down and reviews them each evening; short lists survive real days.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: It was Friday evening, the science chart on the water cycle was due Monday, and Elizabeth's little brother was banging a spoon on a pot in the next room. She unrolled the big sheet and stared at it. So much white. She sharpened three pencils, wandered to the balcony, came back and sat down with her chin on her arms. Her mother Sarita looked in. “Don't do the whole chart. Draw just one cloud, at the top left,” she said. Elizabeth drew a cloud. Then she added rain under it because that was easy. By bedtime she had three boxes drawn, and the white sheet no longer looked so large.

qa.q: What did Sarita ask Elizabeth to draw?
qa.a: Sarita asked Elizabeth to draw just one cloud, at the top left.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth sharpen pencils and wander to the balcony?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt overwhelmed by the size of the blank chart and was avoiding it, since she could not see where to begin.

qa.q: What worked in Sarita's suggestion?
qa.a: Naming one small first piece gave Elizabeth something to start on, and then the next piece felt possible.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel watching her daughter stare at the paper?
qa.a: Sarita probably feels concerned and patient, wanting to help without doing the chart for Elizabeth.

grounding: A child faces a large project, freezes and wanders off until a first small piece is in view.

subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]
passage: On the call, Tanuja held up the social studies chapter, twenty-four pages, and let it flop on the bed. “I can't,” she told Rashmi. “Every time I open it I just see how much there is.” She had already refilled her water bottle three times. Rashmi, who was also stuck on the group map project, said, “Okay, I'll only do the border of the map. Tonight. You only read the first page and underline three words.” Tanuja groaned, but she opened to page one. The pencil felt light. By the time the call ended she had underlined five words and made a note of one question for tomorrow.

qa.q: How many pages does the chapter have?
qa.a: The chapter has twenty-four pages.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja refill her water bottle three times?
qa.a: Tanuja was avoiding the chapter because the whole size of it made her feel stuck and unable to start.

qa.q: What small step helped Tanuja begin, and what came next?
qa.a: Rashmi suggested reading only the first page and underlining three words; Tanuja then underlined five words and wrote a question for tomorrow.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be feeling about the group map project?
qa.a: Rashmi also feels stuck and a bit daunted, which is why Rashmi picked just the border to make a start.

grounding: A child sees only the size of a chapter and freezes until a first small piece is in view.

passage:
Monday: Sunaina wrote “study more” at the top of her planner and sat there for forty minutes with the maths book closed. She wasn't sure what “more” meant, so she scrolled her phone and felt worse.

Wednesday: Her deskmate Arnab showed her his planner, where one line read, “Ch. 3, page 41, sums 1 to 5.” Sunaina copied the style. She solved the five sums in twenty minutes.

Saturday: she wrote “Ch. 3, sums 6 to 10, then check answers” and had a tick beside it before lunch. Study felt like something with edges now.

qa.q: What line did Arnab have in his planner?
qa.a: Arnab's line read, “Ch. 3, page 41, sums 1 to 5.”

qa.q: Why did Sunaina scroll her phone on Monday?
qa.a: Sunaina did not know what “more” meant, so she felt stuck and uneasy, and scrolling was easier than sitting with that feeling.

qa.q: What changed between Monday and Wednesday to help Sunaina start?
qa.a: She replaced a vague goal with a first physical action, chapter three, page 41, five sums, which gave her something to grip. 😊

qa.q: What might Arnab think when Sunaina copies his planner style?
qa.a: Arnab may feel pleased and a little proud that a simple habit of his was useful to Sunaina.

grounding: A teenager writes a vague study goal, sits without a start, then a concrete first action makes beginning possible.

passage: “You keep a stub of pencil and a torn card in your shirt pocket, Abhinav, and you asked why. Come, sit. I'm Gautam, and when I was fifteen, I wrote 'study hard' on the calendar above my bed and felt very noble about it. For a week I sat at the desk every evening, opened the book, looked at the ceiling and got up again. I didn't know where to put my hands. My cousin saw me and said, 'What will you do in the first ten minutes?' I said I didn't know. So I wrote: 'Algebra, exercise 4, questions 1 to 5.' Five questions. I could see the end of them. That night the pencil moved, and the ceiling stopped mattering.”

qa.q: What did the narrator write on the calendar at fifteen?
qa.a: At fifteen, Gautam wrote “study hard” on the calendar above the bed.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel at the desk during that week?
qa.a: Gautam felt lost and stuck: opening the book, looking at the ceiling and giving up showed there was nothing concrete to hold on to.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gautam begin?
qa.a: Gautam's cousin asked what Gautam would do in the first ten minutes, and Gautam answered by writing exercise 4, questions 1 to 5.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt asking that question?
qa.a: The cousin was probably concerned and curious, wanting to help without giving the answer, and simply asked what came first.

grounding: A teenager's vague goal leaves the mind with nothing to grip until a concrete first step is written.

passage: Saturday night. Spent the whole day making the perfect thesis schedule: eleven colours, a tab per chapter, deadlines in bold, even little icons for weekends. It looks amazing. Four hours went into it and I felt busy the whole time, almost proud. Parveen messaged asking how the writing was going, and I said “planning stage,” which is true. But when I opened the blank document to start the first paragraph, my stomach dropped and I closed it again and fixed a font colour instead. The sheet is beautiful and I have written nothing. I think the sheet is easier than the first sentence. — Tushar

qa.q: How many colours did Tushar use in the schedule?
qa.a: Tushar used eleven colours in the schedule.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's stomach drop when the blank document opened?
qa.a: Tushar is frightened of the first paragraph, and fixing the schedule feels safer than beginning the actual writing.

qa.q: What small step could Tushar take next instead of adjusting the sheet?
qa.a: Open the document and write one rough sentence or two for the first paragraph, and allow it to be bad.

qa.q: What might Parveen think on hearing “planning stage”?
qa.a: Parveen probably takes it as normal progress and does not know that Tushar has avoided the writing, so a kind follow-up question could help.

grounding: A student builds an elaborate schedule and feels progress while avoiding the frightening first step of writing.

passage:

Asif: great!! made a tracker with 6 colours and a progress bar 😄
Gurleen: nice. how many pages written?

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when the photo of four lines arrives?
qa.a: Gurleen is probably pleased and relieved that Asif started, and perhaps a little amused at the twelve minutes instead of ten. 😊

grounding: A student polishes a tracker to avoid the frightening first step of writing.

subtype: Splitting a project into checkable pieces [Response]
passage: I'm Vandana, and I share a lab table with Tarun. On Monday I noticed Tarun staring at the fifty-page project report, shoulders low. Then Tarun took a pack of index cards and wrote one job on each: “collect data table,” “write the method,” “draw figure 1,” and so on until there were nine, each labelled with a time of under an hour. A phone timer sat beside the cards. After each job Tarun crossed a card off and stacked it on the right. By four, five cards were in that pile, and Tarun looked lighter, humming a little. I couldn't tell for certain what Tarun felt, only that the shoulders had come up.

qa.q: How many cards did Tarun write jobs on?
qa.a: Tarun wrote jobs on nine cards, each labelled with a time of under an hour.

qa.q: What might Tarun have felt by four o'clock?
qa.a: Tarun probably felt lighter and calmer, since the humming and the raised shoulders suggest the dread had eased, though Vandana cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did the card pile give Tarun as the day went on?
qa.a: Every finished card gave real proof of progress, so the report felt smaller and less scary.

qa.q: How does Vandana interpret Tarun's shoulders?
qa.a: Vandana treats the low shoulders as a sign of heaviness at the start and the raised shoulders as relief, but admits only guessing.

grounding: A wise worker divides a large task into pieces under an hour and ticks them off, seen by an observer.

subtype: Splitting a project into checkable pieces [Response]
passage:
Day 1, Sunday. The thirty-slide seminar felt like a mountain, and Hrithik sat in the hostel room with the laptop shut and his stomach tight. He tore a page from a notebook and wrote ten pieces, each one doable in under an hour: outline, slides 1 to 3, one chart, and so on. He ticked “outline” before dinner.

Day 3, Wednesday. Rukmini from his project group called to check in. Six ticks were done. “Feels weirdly light,” Hrithik said.

Day 6, Saturday. The tenth tick went in on a full page of ticks. He practised the talk once aloud and slept easily.

qa.q: How many pieces did Hrithik write on the page?
qa.a: Hrithik wrote ten pieces, each doable in under an hour.

qa.q: Why was Hrithik's stomach tight on the first day?
qa.a: Hrithik was dreading the thirty-slide seminar because the whole job looked huge and he could not see how to finish it.

qa.q: What effect did the ticks have between Sunday and Saturday?
qa.a: Each tick gave Hrithik real evidence of progress, so the dread shrank from a mountain to a page of finished pieces.

qa.q: What might Rukmini think when Hrithik says it feels weirdly light?
qa.a: Rukmini probably feels relieved and glad that Hrithik is on track, since Rukmini called to check in on the group work.

grounding: A wise worker splits a large task into checkable pieces, and each completed piece lowers dread over several days.
